item.title: The Perennial Problem with Willpower
item.description:
Self-Control

The Perennial Problem with Willpower

What is "willpower" and why it doesn't it work?

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Will is something different than conscious intention and willpower.
  • Willpower tends to be undermined and weakened by unconscious intentionality.
  • Willpower can be strengthened by becoming more conscious of one's true will.
Freud's famous couch
Source: Wikimedia Commons

What is "willpower"? Why is it so difficult to overcome certain problems or attain one's personal goals through the assertion of willpower? What makes it so challenging, for instance, to lose weight, stop procrastinating, or quit drinking or using drugs, despite our best efforts? Or to exercise regularly, meditate, eat better, or get sufficient sleep—despite knowing that doing such things would be in our best interest? We try repeatedly to succeed in such efforts, with the best intentions, but inevitably seem to either fall short or fail. As St. Paul the Apostle laments, "I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do I do not do, but what I hate I do."

What goes wrong? What happens to our so-called willpower? Willpower is commonly defined by the dictionary as the ability to control one's own actions, emotions, thoughts, impulses, or urges and refers to the "strength of one's will, especially in the exercise of self-control." When we are unsuccessful in such efforts, we typically attribute this failure to an absence of willpower. We also tend to attribute such apparent weakness to a lack of moral fiber, will, inner strength, or self-discipline. We tend to blame ourselves and feel guilty for this perceived weakness, which gradually erodes our self-esteem, integrity, and sense of agency. But, in fact, it is a far more profound phenomenon, caused by the inner conflict between our intentions and intentionality. The real underlying problem is that we are not of one mind on these matters. We are a house divided.

Will vs. Willpower

As previously discussed (see my prior post), the concept and experiential discovery of one's will is central to successful psychotherapy of any sort. But, when used in this sense, "will" is something different from what we commonly mean by "willpower." Otto Rank understood that the human will cannot not be expressed in some form or another, is communicated either constructively or destructively, positively or negatively, and that when it cannot be expressed productively or creatively, it becomes neurotic or psychotic, manifesting itself destructively or negatively in the form of what Rank (1936) called "counter-will." So, what is this Rankian notion of will? And how is it different from what we call willpower?

As described by one of Rank's biographers, psychiatrist E.J. Lieberman (1993), "Will represents the life center of the human being, something primal and ultimate." Another biographer, Jessie Taft (1958), writes, "Will is not merely the drive of a predominant instinct or combination of instincts; it is that central integration [and expression] of the forces of the individual which exceeds the sum of the parts."

So-called willpower is an expression of what we believe to be our will or true intentions; but, in reality, it typically stems solely from what the ego, persona, or conscious personality desires, because this, for most of us, is the part of ourselves with which we most strongly identify. But our willpower tends to be sabotaged by what we do not know, or want to know, about ourselves, i.e., the unconscious. This is what undermines and renders willpower weak, impotent, and frequently ineffective.

Rank's ( 1936) "Will Therapy," in some ways a precursor to today's existential therapy, sought to cultivate in the patient or client the capacity to express their will, rather than mere willpower, constructively and creatively in the world. But how is this actually accomplished?

Intentions vs. Intentionality

One way of thinking about this exceedingly common conundrum regarding willpower is to differentiate between one's intentions and intentionality. Intentions consist of what we more or less consciously want or choose to do, whereas intentionality includes both our conscious and unconscious intentions.

Discerning and determining one's true intentionality in life is essential to the ability to freely assert one's will constructively or creatively in the world; that is, if one chooses to do so. This is one of the fundamental goals in contemporary existential therapy. As Rollo May (1969) writes, psychotherapy "ought to be the place par excellence of experiencing intentions and their implied actions and meaning ... without the patient having to transform this into overt behavior." In other words, patients need the opportunity to explore, experience, and verbally express both their conscious intentions and unconscious intentionality within the comparatively safe therapeutic container and within what May (1969) calls the "structure of consciousness," rather than reflexively acting them out in the world. Discerning one's deeper intentionality or will in any given situation is a prerequisite to eventually determining what to do with it in outer reality.

"The road to hell is paved with good intentions."

What is the psychological significance of this saying? While our conscious intentions typically are direct expressions of the ego or persona, our intentionality includes the primitive or primal desires, impulsions, urges, or wishes of what Freud (1950) called the id; what Jung (1961) called the shadow; or what May (1969) called the daimonic (Diamond, 1996).

Our intentionality sometimes initially appears as counter-will, as resistance or opposition to our conscious intentions. We want to say yes to something or someone, yet we say no instead. We intend to act one way, but behave in another. Cognition is overruled by emotion. Or vice versa. We find ourselves doing the polar opposite of what we consciously and conscientiously say, think, or feel we want to, often with disastrous consequences. Then, we scratch our heads wondering what just happened.

It is an extremely confusing, frustrating, and humbling experience. But it brings the beginning of psychological wisdom. We are forced to acknowledge that we are not the master in our own house; there are powerful forces at work within us that transcend and trump our conscious intentions. There is still much to learn about ourselves. We are far more complicated and complex creatures than we ever thought.

Exercising the Will of the Whole Person

Human will, while innate, must be discovered, discerned, refined, and then, like a muscle, creatively exercised. For Rank, neurosis, counter-will, or lack of what we call willpower, is the consequence of not being able to know, accept, and direct one's will constructively and consistently.

To discern one's intentionality is to experience and discover what one truly wants, rather than what one thinks one wants, feels one wants, or even wants to want. It refers to the will of the whole person. Intentionality underpins, and frequently undermines, conscious intention because it taps into the inherent, holistic, organic, instinctual wisdom within, including that of the unconscious and the body.

Whatever our true intentions and intentionality may be, even when they seem antithetical to who we believe ourselves to be, we need to acknowledge and accept them as part of ourselves. And try to reconcile them as best we can. Discerning and discovering our intentionality demands both courage and integrity. Integrity can be understood as unity of the personality. It implies being brutally honest with ourselves about both our intentions and intentionality; what motivates us, and what that says about who we truly are. This is never an easy and not always pleasant pursuit. But it can provide us with a capacity to accomplish things that simple willpower never could.

item.title: Coping After Brain Injury in the Real World vs. the Research
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

Coping After Brain Injury in the Real World vs. the Research

Personal Perspective: Brain injury can limit coping skills.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Active coping strategies improve resilience post-injury, but can be hard to access.
  • Brain injury hampers flow, impacting acquired skills and coping abilities.
  • Finding supportive human connections is crucial for adaptive coping post-brain injury.
Source: klimkim/Pixabay

Last time, I wrote about what the research says regarding coping after brain injury. This week, I want to analyze how well this research dovetails with a real-world example (mine).

The American Psychological Association defines coping as “the use of cognitive and behavioral strategies to manage the demands of a situation when these are appraised as taxing or exceeding one’s resources or to reduce the negative emotions and conflict caused by stress.”

As I noted last time, Cardile et al. wrote, “Research has shown that patients with ABI who use active coping strategies and are problem-oriented face the disease with greater resilience and a sense of self-efficacy and report fewer symptoms.” Sasse et al. in 2014 divided coping strategies into adaptive action/distraction versus maladaptive trivialization/resignation. Bryant et al. in 2000 identified avoidance as a maladaptive coping strategy.

By damaging affect, emotional control, and cognitions, brain injury drastically reduces one’s resources and access to active coping strategies.

I faced this reality after my brain injury. Yet according to the research, my resilient approach of facing my problems, seeking to understand them instead of trivializing and avoiding, and persistently looking for solutions aligned with better coping.

Pre-Injury Coping Strategy

My neurorehab stress management course determined that my top coping strategy prior to my brain injury was reading. Unfortunately, the injury destroyed it. Reading contains elements of distraction—escaping reality into another world—and action, e.g., accumulating knowledge about one’s injury and learning what others do to cope, heal, and reintegrate into society. Any strategy that allows one to enter flow—a state I lost after brain injury—intrinsically rewards and contains elements of action and distraction. But what happens when your injury eliminates automaticity, long-held skills, and cognitions like memory and concentration? You can’t enter flow. And you end up using coping strategies that require no skills and no ability to retain habits.

That’s what happened to me.

Post-Injury Maladaptive Coping

I fell back on the one coping strategy I could use: eating—specifically, organic dark chocolate—whenever I was in physical or psychological pain.

Eating, though, is maladaptive. Unlike reading or television, which can distract for hours, eating distracts only momentarily, necessitating repetition, which worsens health.

Challenges With Diet, Stress, and Weight

My GP diagnosed me with diabetes in 2009 and prescribed a low-glycemic diet. I had been eating the low-glycemic way before my brain injury but had forgotten about it, and no one in my life reminded me.

An adaptive coping personality does not compensate for a brain that requires others to fill in functional gaps. Yet lacking are standardized professional responses to helping an isolated patient replace maladaptive coping strategies with realistic ones that are doable within a person’s injury-created limitations and to buttress effective coping strategies regularly.

My GP referred me to a physical trainer familiar with heart issues in concussed elite athletes. This person modified my diet further and developed an individualized exercise regimen that led to me no longer retaining water and not having to sleep with my head elevated. The trainer had me provide regular feedback and didn’t sugarcoat diet advice. Too often, I forgot advice because the healthcare professional would provide it once, not bluntly enough, and not to any of my team—assuming that since I’m strong, I don’t need reminding or support to act on it. The trainer didn’t make that mistake.

However, after my time with the trainer ended, my injured brain combined with my never-ending high stress levels meant I struggled to keep my weight off. Being able to bake easier, without needing Post-it notes plastered on my cabinets to remind me of each step, exacerbated the situation. On the one hand, baking distracted me and reinforced cognitions; on the other, I had few to share it with. Hiding cookies and brownies in the freezer doesn’t keep them out of my mouth. Watching shows worked better as a distraction strategy that aligned with my neuro-fatigue, which my parents recognized when they insisted I buy a TV for my bedroom. But it was neither productive nor life-affirming.

Regaining Skills and Adaptive Strategies

Over the years, through neurostimulation and neuromodulation treatments, I regained my reading, memory, concentration, writing, and other skills to the extent that, with healthcare support, I can use reading to lessen negative emotions and sympathetic overdrive, and writing and computer work now distract me after next-gen treatments restored flow somewhat, if only for a few minutes.

When my health improved enough about three to four years into the pandemic, my GP and pain specialist prescribed walking five days per week to manage my diabetes and stress. They increased the time very gradually. They are both strict in ensuring I keep it up; my case manager checks in on my walking every so often. Walking, writing, and reading as adaptive coping strategies partially replace eating now because I healed enough through next-gen treatments and have professional support. When the support wanes over holidays, and I’m tired of being tired, I skip a walk or two and write and read less.

I’m experimenting with how to use reading, writing, distraction, and other life-affirming techniques to stop defaulting to the eating strategy and to use only a small treat to reward accomplishing difficult tasks. Since 2000, I’ve not had a robust conversation about replacing eating with a coping strategy my brain injury will allow. Instead, I’ve had sporadic conversations about my weight and diet. Discussing eating in the context of weight, diet, and exercise is not the same as discussing it in the context of coping with overwhelming situations and emotions. In the absence of a robust approach, eating chocolate or cookies is easier.

At the end of the day, the research misses two crucial points that led to my weight gain, despite my adaptive personality traits and knowledge of active strategies. Unhealed brain injury leads to maladaptive coping strategies by eliminating or preventing healthy skills. And no coping strategy can substitute for a person or inclusive community willing to come alongside and metaphorically carry you when circumstances overwhelm an injured brain.

item.title: Inside a Primate Lab: The Animals and People Who Work There
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Inside a Primate Lab: The Animals and People Who Work There

Lindsay Oliver explains what goes on one lab and how it becomes normalized.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Lindsay Oliver's undercover work at an animal testing facility highlights unpublicized realities.
  • Oliver's book reveal monkeys' individuality along with the struggles and humanity of workers inside the lab.
  • Emerging human-focused technologies signal a shift in research away from animal testing.
Source: Anna Klymenko/Pexels.

The vast majority of people have little to no idea what happens in a research lab. This is what award-winning writer and investigator Lindsay Oliver went undercover—not to stir up discontent, but to find out how the animals are treated and how people adapt to what they're doing.

In her riveting new book, Marshmallows Are Their Favorite: Undercover at a Primate Lab, Oliver reports what went on at a primate lab and offers a unique and largely unknown story about its nonhuman residents and the humans who work there.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Marshmallows Are Their Favorite, and how did you come up with the eye-catching title?

Lindsay Oliver: Honestly, I wrote this book because I owe it to the monkeys. When I first walked into that facility and saw cages lining the cinderblock walls, with monkeys watching me through the bars, I knew almost immediately that I needed to write about it. Most people will never be allowed inside a primate lab, and I felt a heavy responsibility to tell these stories.

We all have favorites, and a favorite is personal. That is part of why I landed on Marshmallows Are Their Favorite. It tells you there is an individual there with preferences, opinions, and things they look forward to. I wanted readers to see the monkeys as individuals before they even opened the book.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

LO: Like many kids, I wanted to be a veterinarian growing up. Ironically, college was my first exposure to animal testing and what would have been required of me to be a vet. For the kid who walked out of a high school science class to protest dissecting a frog, this presented a fairly significant problem.

I couldn't reconcile the two, so I walked away and became an undercover animal cruelty investigator instead. The investigation in the book was my very first lab case, and I had no idea how profoundly I would connect with the monkeys behind those walls.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

LO: I know “everyone” is an obnoxious answer, but that’s what the monkeys deserve. I really want to reach people who would never assume that a book about a primate lab is for them. You can pick it up for the undercover element, covert cameras, the double life, the close calls, or the surprising relationships I built with my coworkers.

Source: Ender Press/with permission.

I also hope the book reaches people who work inside labs, especially those who feel conflicted or have been told that caring too much makes them bad at their jobs. It isn’t true. And to the person who sees “primate lab” and thinks, "That sounds too difficult for me to read": I wrote it with you in mind.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

The book looks at what happens when something profoundly wrong becomes ordinary. The facility is in the middle of a town. It could be any town. A Target on one corner, a Starbucks on another, and on another, thousands of monkeys locked in cages. The lab is a workplace, which sounds obvious until you are standing inside it. People clocked in, complained about schedules, gossiped, flirted, and planned their weekends while monkeys screamed and pounded on the walls of their cages. What felt surreal to me was just another Tuesday at the lab.

Part of what makes that normalcy possible is identifying the monkeys by numbers or “subjects,” but these are highly intelligent, sensitive beings. They have distinct personalities, fears, and very strong opinions. Bo, for example, ate everything I handed him except the pretzels, which he threw to the ground as though personally offended by them. It’s through these little moments that you get to know them. And that changes you.

The people were more complicated than I expected, too. I went in assuming the employees were comfortable with what happened there. Some acted like they were, but I wasn’t convinced. Many cared a lot about the monkeys, found small ways to make their lives better, or struggled with what their jobs required of them.

The book also explores the strange reality of undercover work, which is far less James Bond and far more dingy hotels, microwave meals, and equipment that refuses to stay covert. I want readers to walk through those doors with me, get to know the monkeys and the people around them, and come away questioning how any of this became ordinary.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

LO: Many books examine animal experimentation through science, ethics, or policy. While those are all incredibly helpful and needed, mine takes readers through an undercover employee entrance.

I became the inexperienced new technician, learned the routines, wore hidden cameras, made friends, and tried to help the monkeys without revealing why I was really there. Readers get to discover the facility as I did, from getting hired through my final shift.

It’s a story, not a report. There are close calls, strange workplace dynamics, moments of humor, and a relationship that gets a little too close. Facts can show the scale and systemic impact of an industry. I wanted this book to show what it feels like to be inside one.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about the lives of these animals they will re-evaluate their views on the use of nonhumans in this sort of research?

LO: Absolutely. I knew very little about what actually happens inside an animal lab before working in one, and it impacted me on a level I didn’t know was possible.

This book isn't about the industry's scientific failures, but those failures matter to animals and people. The public has been told this is life-saving research: it might hurt some animals, but it's worth it for medical progress. Yet the FDA's own 2025 roadmap for reducing animal testing states: "Over 90% of drugs that appear safe and effective in animals do not go on to receive FDA approval in humans predominantly due to safety and/or efficacy issues." That number doesn't fit the narrative we’ve been sold. And too much of it comes down to habit and inertia.

Continuing to rely on methods that poorly predict human outcomes harms animals and delays the cures we all want. The good news is that science is changing, and the FDA and NIH are beginning to prioritize technologies built around human biology. The challenge now is turning policy into practice. My hope is that meeting these monkeys gives people a reason to act.

item.title: How to Define a Genius
item.description:
Intelligence

How to Define a Genius

Is genius a gift, serendipity, or something else?

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Many renowned geniuses showed little promise in their youth but transformed their potential over time.
  • Genius isn’t merely high IQ; it’s about groundbreaking contributions to a field or understanding.
  • Genius emerges from harnessing giftedness with education, motivation, and opportunity.
Albert Einstein
Source: Needpix.com

In surveying the landscape of current scientific knowledge about giftedness, I discovered the work of Rena F. Subotnik, an American psychologist and a prominent scholar in giftedness, talent development, and gifted education. Subotnik argues that giftedness should not be thought of simply as possessing an unusually high IQ or an exceptional ability in childhood. Early potential must be transformed through education, opportunity, motivation, and other psychosocial factors into increasingly sophisticated expertise and, in rare cases, eminence (her term for genius).

Notable Geniuses Who Defied Early Expectations

While people like Marie Curry, Mozart, or Picasso were conspicuously gifted as children, most gifted children do not rise to the level of geniuses. Some may become very successful but not geniuses.

The converse is also true. Many children who reach genius status later in life showed little promise in their youth.

Thomas Edison struggled with conventional schooling, while Albert Einstein, despite his early mathematical ability, failed the general portion of the entrance examination to the Swiss Federal Polytechnic at age 16.

William Shakespeare received only the standard grammar-school education until his mid-teens, when he had to quit to help the family financially. Importantly, there is no historical evidence of extraordinary literary precocity in his childhood. Yet he became arguably the greatest playwright who ever lived.

Leonardo da Vinci had even less formal education. Born illegitimate, he was instructed mainly in ordinary spoken and written Italian rather than in Latin and did not study Greek, philosophy, or mathematics available to children of nobility. Still, da Vinci became one of the greatest painters and most diverse scientific minds in history.

Defining a "Genius"

Giftedness and genius are not synonymous. Historically, both became enmeshed with IQ testing, but scientists now realize that this was a mistake. A child with an IQ of 160 is extraordinarily gifted, but we don't automatically call that child a genius. Einstein is considered a genius not because someone measured his IQ but because he changed our understanding of space and time.

Apart from the studies on Einstein’s brain, which only showed greater connectivity between the two hemispheres, there is surprisingly little neuroscience that explores “genius” itself, for the obvious reason that the designation “genius” is generally retrospective. Hardly anyone is considered a genius in their lifetime. The strongest academic literature therefore comes from two overlapping areas: exceptional creativity and high intelligence.

The authors of these studies concluded that highly creative people do not necessarily possess different brain machinery. They may be unusually good at coordinating two normally competing mental processes: Letting the mind roam freely enough to produce unexpected ideas while maintaining enough control to recognize which ideas are worth pursuing.

Historical Context and Evolution of the Term "Genius"

Eric Weiner, in his book, The Geography of Genius, describes how creative genius flourished in specific places at specific times in history, such as Athens in 450 BC, Renaissance Florence, or Silicon Valley in the present, to name a few. These places provided opportunities to engage in stimulating intellectual frisson with other like-minded friends and rivals in a society that valued their achievements and provided them with financial support.

The Latin "genius" originally referred not to exceptional intelligence but to a guiding or generative spirit associated with a person. Only much later did the word migrate from a person having a genius to a person being a genius.

The Myth of the "Mad Genius"

Popular culture has long cherished the image of the “mad genius," brilliant but eccentric, emotionally unstable, socially unconventional, and hovering somewhere near the border between inspiration and madness.

Many authorities report that highly creative scientists and artists tend to be open to experience, unconventional, self-confident, driven, and independent, while often being somewhat less conscientious in the conventional sense. However, any serious mental disorder itself would interfere rather than further the creative process. “What allows genius to flower is not neurosis, but its opposite, 'ego strength,' meaning among other things ordinary, Sunday-school virtues such as tenacity and, above all, the ability to survive disappointment," wrote cultural critic and author Joan Acocella.

The Role of Serendipity in Genius

Consider the career of Sir Alexander Fleming, the discoverer of penicillin. He chose to attend St. Mary’s Hospital Medical School in London, partly because, as a teenager, he had played water polo against its team and made some friends there. While there, Fleming became an excellent shot, so his supervisor wanted to keep him at St. Mary’s on its rifle team. Thus encouraged, Fleming stayed at St. Mary’s to study bacteriology.

Then came the famous accident. A mold contaminated one of his bacterial cultures. Plenty of scientists might simply have thrown the spoiled dish away. Fleming noticed something peculiar: bacteria were not growing around the mold. He pursued the observation, and penicillin was born. People liked him, admired him, and wanted to keep him around. Doors opened. He was invited to enter. He entered.

The Complexity of Geniuses

Not all geniuses are like Fleming. Geniuses may not always be “nice” people or easy to get along with. They have their faults like the rest of us. But they have something that induces other people to take an interest in them. That “something” might be charm, confidence, usefulness, persuasiveness, or the extraordinary quality of the work itself.

What we know for certain is that genius is not about psychometric tests or brain architecture or creativity, though all these are contributing factors. In the scientific field. It is a sudden flash sometimes referred to as a "lightbulb moment." A connection is made that no one else ever made, like Newton watching the apple fall. Or it is the gradual development in a person with talent and personality who patiently and often single-mindedly keeps perfecting their craft over time. A good example is Toni Morrison, whose linguistic originality, psychological depth, and treatment of history transformed American literature. She won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature.

Life throws you a pass. Catching it shows you are gifted. Convert it to a touchdown, and you enter the pantheon of geniuses. Giftedness is potential; genius is what you do with it.

Adapted from an article that also appears in The Globe and Mail.

item.title: A Powerful Practice to Help Process Regret
item.description:
Cognition

A Powerful Practice to Help Process Regret

Could an iconic phone booth in Japan help us heal from our most painful regrets?

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Regret can be a tenacious emotion. It's also a universal one.
  • People often regret inaction, or have moral and relational regrets.
  • Japan's Wind Phone, used to "communicate" with those who have died, offers a path to healing from regret.

Sometimes wisdom appears in the least expected places. I was walking down a busy main street in Cambridge, MA, past a homeless man who had requisitioned a park bench as his temporary abode. His hand-written sign stopped me mid-step: “Pain is temporary, regret is forever.”

The feeling is a resoundingly familiar one. About a year ago, the renowned restaurateur Keith McNally penned a best-seller whose title summed up the sentiment unforgettably: I Regret Almost Everything. As a clinical psychologist, I am often humbled by how difficult it is for people to let go of regret. People often ruminate on this emotion, returning to the story again and again over the course of a long treatment.

What Makes Us Feel Regret?

I took a look at the recent research. Regret is thought to be a universal emotion. However, it can help us learn from our mistakes, as acknowledging the mistake can guide us to make better choices. There is a wide range of what people regret. There's inaction—not taking a chance in a relationship or a work opportunity. There are also moral regrets—not doing the right thing—and connection regrets, neglecting or breaking relationships.

As I reflect on my caseload, I see these themes again and again. One patient, now in her 80s, frequently brings up the suicide of her brother, although she did everything she could to keep him alive. And because we have revisited this story, I worry that I have nothing new to add. Another client regrets that she didn’t spend more time with her best friend, who died a long, agonizing death from Alzheimer’s.

I have often wondered why regret is so tenacious. And, more practically and importantly, what can we do to ease the pain? A gifted Zen Master that I study with, Roshi Jon Joseph, recently wrote a blog post that inspired me. In this evocative essay he talks about a telephone booth outside of Otsuchi, Japan that is called the “Wind Phone.” It is not connected to any telephone lines. It was created after an earthquake in 2011 which killed ten percent of the population. Thousands of people have used it to communicate with a loved one who has died.

I kept thinking about the potential that the white phone booth held. Obviously, I couldn’t go to Japan with my patient. However, I had spent years in graduate school studying and writing about cross-cultural and indigenous forms of healing for a major research study on human potential. Because of this background, I wasn’t bound by thinking in the traditional Western psychological tradition of Freudian theory or cognitive behavioral therapy.

One day, my patient told me that she needed to talk about her friend “Mary.” She hadn’t been sleeping again and she was having nightmares. Therapy wasn’t helping: Was it time for medication?

“Let’s try one more thing” I suggested, and told her about the Wind Phone, (my equivalent of a Hail Mary pass, bringing in some needed humor here). We imagined that a Wind Phone was in my office. She mimed picking up the phone and words rushed out: She had been haunted by what she didn’t say; she loved Mary so much; she still talks to her in her mind, especially at night. She misses her terribly. She went on and on with things that had been unsaid and unspoken. At the end of the conversation, we were both in tears. That was months ago.

I asked her recently how she was feeling about Mary’s death. “I don’t know what it was about the Wind Phone,” she shrugged, “but I feel like I really connected with her, that we actually spoke, and that awful ache is resolved.” She paused. “Thanks for thinking outside the usual phone booth,” she joked.

We can never say what makes something healing, but I have tried the idea of the phone booth with a number of people and have tried it myself, working with unresolved issues around my mother’s recent death and my significant regrets. In fact, it turns out that “wind phones” have been constructed all over the world. There is something in this metaphor that speaks deeply to people no matter what their cultural heritage might be.

Guiding Principles for Processing Regret

As I work with people to help process regret I have been guided by 3 principles:

  1. Acknowledge it. Don’t suppress what happened.
  2. Practice self-compassion. We all are imperfect and have regrets. As one Zen master quipped, “Life is one mistake after another.”
  3. Create a cognitive reframe. We can learn from our mistakes, and as the meditation teachers tell us, we can always start again.

I don’t believe that regret is forever. More importantly, I think that healing is always possible, but rarely simple.

item.title: One Simple Way to Reduce Romantic Conflict
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

One Simple Way to Reduce Romantic Conflict

Use the "power of the pause" to de-escalate emotion.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • Negative affect increases the likelihood of aggression.
  • Emotion drives behavior, and facial expression can provoke conflict.
  • Pausing de-escalates the perception of negativity, which can de-escalate impulsive behavior.
Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

Most romantic partners can identify with relational highs and lows. Yet when there is trouble in paradise, calming the storm may be easier than we think—in the moment.

Research explores the power of the pause—taking a “time out” to de-escalate disagreement.

Interrupting Emotional Negativity

Obviously, as a career prosecutor, my message is that domestic violence should be reported to law enforcement. But many couples struggle with verbal aggression and toxic communication patterns, which are enormously destructive to relational quality. Thankfully, there are strategies to reduce negativity.

Annah G. McCurry et al. (2024) explored the link between negative emotion and aggression during couples’ conflict. They recognize that expressed emotion drives behavior and negative affect increases the likelihood of aggression. They note that even the perception of a partner’s emotion can impact aggression, which can lead to what they refer to as a violence escalation cycle. As many couples are aware, this pattern can become a significant problem when one or both partners struggle with emotion regulation, considering the link between poor emotional regulation and the chance of aggressive behavior.

How does escalation occur? McCurry et al. found that experiencing negative emotion predicts reactive aggression between partners. Prototypic displays of negative emotion through facial affect compound the effect, which produces dramatic alterations in patterns of aggression depending on partner expressiveness. But there is a way to interrupt this process.

Breaking Bad Habits by Taking a Break

Seeking to reduce aggression, McCurry et al. imposed temporal delays in the form of experimental forced breaks that decreased negative emotional arousal and limited impulsive action. Sure enough, they found that breaks, whether forced or elected (where participants chose to extend the forced break time), reduced aggression, demonstrating how interventions that are focused on preventing impulsive action during periods of partner provocation can reduce aggression.

Regarding the expressiveness of one or both partners, McCurry et al. observed an 86 percent increase in aggression when both partners were expressing negative emotion compared to when neither partner was doing so. They also found indications of patterned behavior and reciprocity, noting that the dynamic interaction between partners over time showed that couples begin to match each other’s aggression.

Their most important discovery, however, was that the introduction of a short delay post-provocation reduced aggression, which can be a powerful, practical intervention aimed at reducing aggression between partners. Regarding timing, they found that time spans ranging from 5 to 15 seconds resulted in similar reductions in negative emotion and aggression, although they also found that participants who chose to take extra time before responding experienced a further decrease in negative emotion and exhibited less aggression. They note the practical value of their findings—that training individuals to take voluntary breaks may constitute an effective strategy for aggression reduction.

Practicing Patience Through Pausing

Apparently, there is power in taking a pause, assuming a mutual time-out to allow both partners to take a breath. As most people know from other situations, a break in the action often diverts the path. Couples desiring to break cycles of negativity can proactively prevent conflict from escalating if agreed-upon breaks are practiced as an option. And for couples who choose to augment interpersonal strategies in their personal lives, professional help is available.
